## TL;DR

Reproduced the Hub’s broken dark-mode sidebar on a real macOS build, fixed the appearance mismatch and narrow sidebar, and verified the app in dark System appearance and forced Light appearance. The Hub built and its macOS test suite passed; `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed. Adding `127.0.0.1:7171` succeeded, showed Healthy, opened the RepoOS sign-in page, and remained saved after quitting and relaunching the test build. Authentication into the RepoOS UI still requires Nick’s login.

## Work and rationale

The reported failure was real and reproducible. The app launched without crashing. In macOS Dark appearance, its sidebar was solid white while the detail pane was dark; the server names and URLs were light and therefore nearly invisible. The count badges had poor contrast, the sidebar was too narrow to show server addresses, and the selected `localhost:7405` server was marked Offline with a “Start local server” message.

The root cause was inconsistent appearance handling. `ServerSidebarView` and the app shell supplied a literal white background for the System setting even though SwiftUI used the system color scheme. Native window surfaces were also being forced to concrete colors, so the effective SwiftUI appearance and AppKit surfaces could disagree. The fix resolves `NSColor.windowBackgroundColor` for the effective Aqua or Dark Aqua appearance, then uses the same appearance-aware color for the shell, sidebar, and server tab strip. The application delegate refreshes AppKit layer colors when macOS broadcasts an interface theme change. Server names explicitly use the primary semantic foreground, and the sidebar width now allows names and URLs to remain visible.

History points to `bf428a0f0` (“fix(macos): render light native chrome explicitly”, 2026-09-26) as the introduction of explicit light native chrome; the hard-coded white behavior predates the reported late-October onset. The macOS commits since 2026-10-15 did not reveal a server API contract change that explains this visual failure. The health probe uses the entered server origin’s `/api/health` endpoint. This machine had no listener on port 7405, while the local server on 7171 responded Healthy, so the Offline state was correct for the saved 7405 URL rather than evidence of a stale row or a probe aimed at the wrong URL.

Verification used a separately identified test build so the installed Hub was not quit. Window screenshots were inspected before and after the fix. In dark System appearance, the sidebar became dark with readable names and URLs, clear badges, and no clipped right edge. In forced Light appearance, it became light with dark readable text and clear badges. The setting was restored to System. I added `127.0.0.1:7171` in the app; it showed Healthy and opened the RepoOS login page. After quitting and relaunching the test app, the server was still listed and Healthy. The added alias is saved in the user’s Hub registry and remains there. No login was attempted; authenticated UI beyond the sign-in page needs Nick’s credentials.

## Approaches tried

I first built and launched the current scheme to reproduce the symptom rather than infer it from source. I inspected the native appearance setup and SwiftUI surfaces, then centralized semantic background resolution so all relevant surfaces agree with the active scheme. I widened the sidebar and made the row label’s semantic foreground explicit. A new appearance unit test checks that semantic system window surfaces differ between Aqua and Dark Aqua and that forced light/dark settings resolve to the expected appearance.

The initial unit-test run exposed machine-dependent discovery tests: they implicitly read the real `~/.repoos/servers` registry, which prevented fallback-scan fixtures from running. I isolated those tests with a unique nonexistent registry directory and strengthened the populated-registry test to fail if fallback scanning occurs. This keeps tests independent of Nick’s local server list.

## Challenges and blockers

The normal macOS Debug build succeeded. Xcode printed a CoreDevice private-framework symbol warning and a CoreSimulator version warning; neither prevented the macOS build or test run. The full `xcodebuild ... test` run passed after test isolation. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` also passed its changed-path validation, including format, lint, build, and UI smoke checks.

The 7405 endpoint was unavailable in this environment, so its Offline state could not be turned into a Healthy demonstration; the app’s correct response was confirmed by checking listeners and successfully probing the available local server on 7171. Opening that server reached the sign-in screen. Nick must authenticate to verify content behind login. No crash occurred, so there is no crash log or crash text to report.

## Key learnings

System appearance needs to be resolved at the point where AppKit colors are converted to concrete layer colors; assigning a fixed white value for a System preference breaks dark mode. Reusing a semantic appearance-aware background across the SwiftUI shell, sidebar, and tab strip prevents mismatched panes. Discovery tests should explicitly control both registry contents and fallback scanning rather than inherit a developer’s home-directory state. Finally, “Start local server” is an accurate status when the entered localhost port has no listener; testing a known live URL distinguishes that condition from an API-path regression.
